content: The process of organizing, planning, coordinating, and delivering communication and engagement strategies involves utilizing various methods and approaches. These efforts are systematically assessed based on evidence from recent emergencies to determine what has been effective and what has not. Monitoring and evaluation are integral components of this process. These guidelines are intended for policymakers and decision-makers responsible for managing emergencies, particularly those addressing public health aspects. They are also designed for practitioners involved in risk communication before, during, and after health emergencies. Other groups expected to use these guidelines include frontline responders, local, national, and international development partners, civil society organizations, the private sector, and all entities involved in emergency preparedness and response. The development of these guidelines began in October 2014 with the establishment of an Internal Steering Group (ISG) and the commissioning of a flash literature review. This review provided an overview of existing Emergency Risk Communication (ERC) guidance and identified areas for improvement. The review highlighted gaps in guidance, such as the use of mobile technologies, evaluation research, barriers to preparedness, ERC in low-income countries, capacity building during preparedness phases, and the application of evidence and past experiences to improve ERC. In early 2015, a Guideline Development Group (GDG) was formed, comprising experts in risk communication, disaster preparedness, response, and health emergencies. The GDG held its first meeting in Geneva, Switzerland, in June 2015 to discuss the findings of the literature review. They defined the scope of the guidelines, identified areas requiring further investigation, and framed questions to guide a systematic evidence search. Twelve questions were developed to guide evidence reviews, which were commissioned in 2016 and completed by January 2017. The findings were presented to the GDG, which met in February 2017 to formulate recommendations. These recommendations were based on evidence-to-decision tables that analyzed what worked, what did not, values, preferences, resource use, and equity considerations. An anonymous electronic vote was conducted to establish the initial group position, and the recommendations were ultimately agreed upon by the majority, with dissenting views reflected in remarks or modifications. An external group of ERC practitioners, emergency responders, academics, and policymakers reviewed the recommendations. Their comments, changes, and additions were further reviewed by the GDG, which finalized the recommendations. The recommendations are categorized into three main areas: (A) Building trust and engaging with affected populations, (B) Integrating ERC into health and emergency response systems, and (C) ERC practice. Category A: Building Trust and Engagement To build trust, risk communication interventions should be linked to accessible services, be transparent, timely, and easy to understand, acknowledge uncertainties, address affected populations, promote self-efficacy, and use multiple platforms and channels. Communication should explicitly include information about uncertainties and what is known or unknown at a given time. Identifying trusted community members and involving them in decision-making ensures interventions are collaborative, contextually appropriate, and community-owned. Category B: Integrating ERC into Systems Risk communication must function within health and emergency preparedness and response systems. ERC should have a strategic role in global and national emergency leadership teams, supported by a defined and sustained budget as part of core emergency funding. Regular training and preparation of ERC personnel should focus on coordination across stakeholders. Category C: ERC Practice Strategic communication planning involves assessing needs, setting objectives, implementing targeted interventions, and monitoring and evaluating activities to improve public awareness and influence behavior. Social media can be used to engage the public, monitor rumors, and facilitate local-level responses. Messaging should be culturally adapted, pretested with intended audiences, and periodically reviewed as emergencies evolve. Consistent messaging from different sources should emerge early in an outbreak and promote specific, actionable steps for individuals to protect their health. The guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based recommendations for effective ERC. They do not provide step-by-step instructions but offer a framework for the elements of effective ERC. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews of quantitative and qualitative evidence, supplemented by rapid reviews of recent grey literature to ensure no relevant evidence was missed. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed these guidelines to address gaps in risk communication during major outbreaks and emergencies, such as the West African Ebola virus outbreak (2014–2015) and the global Zika virus outbreak (2015–2016). The guidelines aim to provide the most up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations for communicating risk in health emergencies, enabling individuals and communities to make informed decisions to protect their health and well-being.
